name: Hydrogen gas
blurb: Each hydrogen has 1 hand. They hold hands, and now neither has an empty hand. The lightest molecule there is.
uses: Adding hydrogen to fuels at refineries, ammonia, fuel cells, liquid hydrogen rocket fuel.

lens.rocket: Liquid H2 (-253 °C) gets the most push per pound of any common rocket propellant. But it's so light that it needs huge tanks.
lens.nexus: Hydrogen is the scarce ingredient at your plant. Polyethylene has only 2 H per carbon, so not every broken piece can fill its hands and become methane.

facts: About 9 of every 10 atoms in the universe are hydrogen. Nearly all of it was made in the first minutes after the Big Bang.
The Sun shines by squeezing hydrogen into helium, about 600 million tons every second.
The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen because the US would not sell Germany helium.

details.what: The smallest, lightest molecule there is: two hydrogen atoms holding hands. A colorless gas with no smell.
details.where: Almost none floats free in our air, because it's light enough to drift up and escape to space. Factories make most of it from natural gas and coal.
details.bonds: The single handshake sits very close to two tiny centers, so it's a strong grip. But the molecules barely pull on each other, so it only turns liquid about 20 degrees above the coldest possible temperature.
details.extra: Hydrogen slips into tiny gaps in some steels and makes them brittle. That's one reason storing and piping hydrogen is harder and costlier than it sounds.

rankWhy: Used to make ammonia and to clean up fuels at refineries. A possible clean fuel.

name: Oxygen gas
blurb: Each oxygen has 2 hands. They hold both hands with each other: a double bond.
uses: Breathing, burning, steelmaking, and liquid oxygen (LOX), what rocket fuel burns with.

lens.rocket: Liquid oxygen is most of the weight of a methane or kerosene rocket. Raptor reportedly burns about 3.6 kg of oxygen per kg of methane.

facts: Liquid oxygen is pale blue, and it gets pulled toward a strong magnet.
By weight, oxygen is the most common element in Earth's crust, a bit under half of all rock.
Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by plants, algae and tiny ocean microbes using sunlight.

details.what: The oxygen we breathe: two oxygen atoms holding both hands. It makes up about 21% of air.
details.where: Every breath, every flame and every rusting nail. Hospitals and steel mills buy it pure, separated out of air that has been chilled into a liquid.
details.bonds: The double grip is solid, but two of its electrons stay unpaired. That makes O2 restless, ready to grab electrons from fuels, metals and food.
details.extra: Carl Scheele and Joseph Priestley each made oxygen in the 1770s. Antoine Lavoisier named it in 1777 and showed that burning means joining with oxygen.

rankWhy: About a fifth of the air. You breathe it, and every fire burns with it.

name: Ozone
blurb: Three oxygens can't all hold hands in a simple, even way. So the shared electrons smear across all three. That awkward grip makes it quick to react.
uses: High-up shield against the sun's UV; cleaning and disinfecting water.
facts: If all the ozone high in the sky were squeezed to ground-level pressure, it would make a layer only about 3 mm thick. That's about two pennies stacked.
Its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'to smell.' The sharp, clean smell near a lightning storm can be ozone.

details.what: A molecule of three oxygen atoms. A pale blue gas, much less steady than the O2 we breathe.
details.where: High in the sky, in the ozone layer, where it soaks up harmful UV light. Near the ground it's a pollutant in hot-weather smog.
details.bonds: Its grips are in between single and double, shared over three atoms. That loose setup lets one oxygen break off easily, which is why ozone attacks rubber, germs and lungs.
details.extra: In 1985 scientists reported a 'hole' in the ozone layer over Antarctica, caused by chlorine from spray cans and coolants. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased those chemicals out, and the layer is slowly healing.

rankWhy: High up, the ozone layer shields life from harmful sunlight.

name: Nitrogen gas
blurb: Each nitrogen has 3 hands, and they hold all three at once: a triple bond. It's one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. That's why N2 barely reacts.
uses: 78% of air; a do-nothing gas used to blanket reactors and tanks.

lens.nexus: At Nexus, nitrogen is flushed through the reactors to push oxygen out. So plastic breaks apart instead of burning.
lens.rocket: Nitrogen gas flushes out lines. It's also the gas pushed out of simple cold-gas thrusters.

facts: Liquid nitrogen boils at -196 °C. One cup of it turns into roughly 700 cups of gas.
Every breath you take is mostly nitrogen, and your body breathes it right back out unused.
Plants can't use it straight from the air either. Lightning and special soil bacteria are nature's main ways to crack that triple bond.

details.what: Two nitrogen atoms locked together. The most common gas in air, with no color, smell or taste.
details.where: Every breath you take, and the puffy air inside a bag of chips, which keeps them from going stale. Liquid nitrogen flash-freezes food and stores samples in labs.
details.bonds: Breaking that triple grip takes a lot of energy, so N2 just floats around doing nothing. Going the other way, nitrogen chemicals that snap back into N2 release a lot of energy. That's why many explosives contain nitrogen.
details.extra: Car airbags fill with nitrogen gas, made in a split second when a solid chemical breaks apart. Older designs used sodium azide for this.

rankWhy: Most of the air. It's also the raw ingredient for all nitrogen fertilizer.

name: Chlorine gas
blurb: Each chlorine has 1 hand. Two chlorines hold hands, and both are satisfied.
uses: Making PVC, cleaning drinking water, bleach.
facts: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas. Its name comes from the Greek word for pale green.
In 1915 at Ypres, chlorine became the first poison gas used on a large scale in war.
Adding chlorine to drinking water in the early 1900s is a big reason diseases like cholera and typhoid became rare.

details.what: Two chlorine atoms holding hands. A heavy, poisonous gas that's harsh to breathe.
details.where: You meet it indirectly: pool sanitizer, household bleach and PVC pipe all trace back to chlorine gas made in factories.
details.bonds: The single grip between two chlorines is fairly weak, and each chlorine badly wants one more electron. So Cl2 splits easily and grabs electrons from germs, dyes and metals. That's the idea behind bleaching.
details.extra: Carl Scheele made chlorine in 1774 but thought it held oxygen. Humphry Davy showed in 1810 that it was its own element and gave it its name.

rankWhy: Keeps drinking water safe and is needed to make PVC.

name: Fluorine gas
blurb: Like chlorine, each has 1 hand, so they hold hands once. Fluorine tugs on electrons harder than any element. So F2 attacks almost anything.
uses: Making uranium hexafluoride, sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and other fluorine chemicals.
facts: Fluorine was so hard to isolate that several chemists were hurt trying. Henri Moissan finally did it in 1886 and later won a Nobel Prize.
It reacts with nearly every element, even the noble gas xenon.
The fluoride in toothpaste is fluorine that has already grabbed an extra electron, so it's calm instead of wild.

details.what: Two fluorine atoms holding hands. A pale yellow gas and the most reactive element in pure form.
details.where: You never meet it free. You meet its tamed forms: fluoride in tap water, Teflon pans, and the coolant gas in air conditioners.
details.bonds: The F-F grip is oddly weak, because the two small atoms crowd each other's electrons. But fluorine makes very strong grips with almost anything else. So F2 swaps partners eagerly.
details.extra: Fluorine is so grabby that even water can't stand up to it. It pulls the hydrogen off water and sets the oxygen free.

name: Bromine
blurb: Each bromine has 1 hand, so two of them hold hands. It's a liquid at room temperature.
uses: Fire-slowing additives, drilling fluids, water treatment.
facts: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
Its name comes from the Greek word for stench. It has a harsh, choking smell.
Royal purple, the ancient dye made from sea snails, has bromine in it.

details.what: Pairs of bromine atoms holding hands. A heavy, dark red-brown liquid that gives off reddish fumes.
details.where: Mostly hidden inside other products, like flame-slowing chemicals in electronics and some hot tub sanitizers. It's pulled from very salty water, such as the Dead Sea.
details.bonds: Bromine atoms are bigger than chlorine's, so the shared pair sits farther out and the grip is weaker. Bigger, softer molecules also cling to each other more, so it's a liquid while chlorine is a gas.
details.extra: Antoine Balard found bromine in 1826 while studying seaweed ash from the salt marshes near Montpellier, France.

name: Iodine
blurb: Each iodine has 1 hand, so two hold hands. The atoms are big and soft, so it's a solid that turns straight into purple vapor.
uses: Germ killer, iodized salt, helping insides show up on X-rays.
facts: Iodine was discovered in 1811 by a French chemist who was making gunpowder ingredients from seaweed ash.
Your thyroid gland needs iodine. Adding it to salt, starting in the US in 1924, made goiter (a swollen neck) rare.
Its name comes from the Greek word for violet, the color of its vapor.

details.what: Pairs of iodine atoms holding hands. Shiny gray-black crystals, the heaviest everyday member of the chlorine family.
details.where: The brown iodine tincture in a first-aid kit, iodized salt and seaweed. Much of the world's supply comes from Chile and Japan.
details.bonds: Iodine's single grip is the weakest in its family, because its atoms are so big. But big, soft electron clouds make the molecules cling to each other, so it's a solid.
details.extra: Iodine turns starch deep blue-black. Schools use a drop of iodine to test foods like bread and potato for starch.

name: Methane
blurb: Carbon has 4 hands and no other carbon to hold. So all 4 hands grab hydrogens. Every hand held: the most settled shape for one carbon.
uses: Natural gas fuel, making hydrogen, rocket fuel.

lens.nexus: The smallest thing your plant makes. It stays a gas even when cooled, and is usually burned to heat the reactor.
lens.rocket: Raptor's fuel. It burns clean (little soot or carbon gunk) and can be made on Mars with the Sabatier reaction.

facts: Natural gas has no smell. Gas companies add a sulfur chemical that smells like rotten eggs so you notice a leak.
Cows burp out methane made by microbes living in their stomachs.
Saturn's moon Titan is so cold that it has lakes and rain made of liquid methane.

details.what: The simplest carbon molecule: one carbon holding four hydrogens. The main gas in natural gas.
details.where: Your gas stove, furnace and water heater. Microbes also make it in landfills, swamps and rice paddies, and it's a strong greenhouse gas.
details.bonds: Its four C-H grips point to the corners of a little pyramid shape, spread as far apart as possible. The molecule is small and even, so molecules barely cling to each other, and it stays a gas until about -162 °C.
details.extra: Natural gas is shipped across oceans as a cold liquid called LNG. Chilled to about -162 °C, it takes up about 600 times less space.

rankWhy: Natural gas: heats homes, makes electricity, and starts the chain to fertilizer and plastics.

name: Ethane
blurb: Two carbons hold hands using one hand each. Each carbon has 3 hands left, and each grabs a hydrogen.
uses: Main raw material for US ethane 'crackers', plants that turn it into ethylene.

lens.nexus: Cheap shale ethane is why most US crackers run on ethane, not naphtha (a light oil). Your plant's oil can stand in for naphtha, so it fits crackers fed on liquid.

facts: Ethane boils at about -89 °C, so on Earth it's always a gas. On frozen Titan it pools in lakes with methane.
It comes out of the ground mixed into natural gas, then gets separated and piped to crackers.

details.what: Two carbons holding hands, each also holding three hydrogens. A colorless gas, the second-biggest part of natural gas.
details.where: You rarely meet it directly. It's split from natural gas and turned into ethylene, which becomes bags, bottles and pipe.
details.bonds: The single C-C grip works like an axle: each end can spin freely. Chemists use this spin as the simplest example of how molecules twist.
details.extra: US ethane output soared with the shale boom. Some of it now crosses the ocean as a chilled liquid to plastics plants in Europe and China.

name: Ethylene
blurb: Each carbon holds 2 hydrogens and the other carbon, with one hand left. So they hold hands twice: a C=C double bond. That second grip is the 'handle' for linking into plastic chains.
uses: The building block of polyethylene; the most-made carbon-based chemical.

lens.nexus: Cracking pulls hydrogen off ethane to make ethylene. Then ethylenes get linked into polyethylene. Your plant partly runs that backwards. But polyethylene breaks into many sizes, not mostly back to ethylene.

facts: Plants make ethylene as a ripening signal. One ripe banana in a bag speeds up the other fruit around it.
Fruit companies pump ethylene into warehouse 'ripening rooms' to time when bananas turn yellow.

details.what: Two carbons holding hands twice, each also holding two hydrogens. A sweet-smelling gas and the starting block of most plastics.
details.where: Polyethylene bags, PVC pipe, antifreeze and polyester clothing all start as ethylene.
details.bonds: A double bond is one strong grip plus a weaker second one. The weaker grip opens easily so other atoms can link on. It also holds the molecule flat, so it can't spin like ethane.
details.extra: In 1923, doctors in Chicago began using ethylene mixed with oxygen to put surgery patients to sleep.

rankWhy: The most-made building block in the plastics industry.

name: Acetylene
blurb: Each carbon holds just 1 hydrogen, leaving 3 hands free. So the carbons hold all 3: a triple bond. Lots of stored energy.
uses: Welding and cutting torches with oxygen (about 3,100 °C flame).
facts: Pure acetylene is unsafe to squeeze into a tank. Welding cylinders are packed with a spongy filler soaked in acetone, and the acetylene dissolves into it.
Old miners' lamps made acetylene by dripping water onto rocks of calcium carbide, then burned the gas for light.

details.what: Two carbons holding three hands together, each with one hydrogen. A gas that burns very hot with pure oxygen.
details.where: Welding shops and metal-cutting torches. It's also a building block for some plastics and chemicals.
details.bonds: The triple grip pulls the two carbons into a short, straight stick. Packing three grips that close strains them, so acetylene reacts readily, unlike nitrogen's calm triple bond.
details.extra: Swedish engineer Gustaf Dalén won the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physics for acetylene lighthouse lamps that switched on and off by themselves with daylight.

name: Propane
blurb: Three carbons in a row. End carbons hold 3 H, the middle one 2.
uses: Heating and grill fuel (LPG), raw material for propylene.

lens.nexus: Part of the light gas that comes off your plant's reactor.

facts: Propane is heavier than air. A leak sinks and collects in low spots like basements.
It boils at about -42 °C. Grill tanks hold it as a liquid under pressure, and it boils into gas when you open the valve.

details.what: Three carbons in a chain, every spare hand holding a hydrogen. A gas that's easy to store as a liquid, sold as LPG.
details.where: Grill tanks, RV stoves, forklifts, patio heaters and rural home heating.
details.bonds: All its grips are single, so there's no weak spot to attack. It just burns. Being a bit bigger than methane, its molecules cling more, so it liquefies with only mild pressure.
details.extra: In 1910, US chemist Walter Snelling separated propane from the lightest part of gasoline. He's often called the father of the propane industry.

rankWhy: Grill and heating gas, and a fuel for forklifts.

name: Propylene
blurb: Three carbons; two hold hands twice. That double grip is where polypropylene chains link.

lens.nexus: Like ethylene, it stays a gas at room temperature. It leaves with the gases that don't turn to liquid.

facts: After ethylene, propylene is the second most important building block for plastics.
Refinery units that crack heavy oil into gasoline make lots of propylene on the side.

details.what: Three carbons where one pair holds hands twice. A gas very much like ethylene, with an extra CH3 branch.
details.where: Polypropylene yogurt cups, car bumpers and carpet fiber. It's also the starting point for acrylic fibers.
details.bonds: The double grip is the reactive spot. In the plastic, that CH3 becomes a branch on every other carbon. The branches change how the chains pack.
details.extra: Propylene and propane boil only a few degrees apart. Separating them takes some of the tallest distillation towers in a plant.

rankWhy: The second big plastics building block after ethylene.

name: Butane
blurb: 4 carbons in a row, spare hands all on H. Straight chains (alkanes) follow CnH(2n+2).
facts: You can see butane sloshing as a liquid in a clear lighter. A little pressure keeps it liquid at room temperature.
It boils at about -1 °C, so a lighter left in freezing cold may barely light.
Its branched twin, isobutane, has the same atoms. It's the cooling gas in many home fridges.

details.what: Four carbons in a chain, every spare hand holding a hydrogen. A gas that turns liquid with light pressure.
details.where: Lighters, camp stove canisters and aerosol sprays. Refiners also blend more of it into gasoline in winter to help cold engines start.
details.bonds: Each extra carbon in a chain makes molecules cling a bit more. That's why methane through butane are gases, but slightly longer chains are liquids at room temperature.
details.extra: Butane's name traces back to butyric acid, the smell of rancid butter, which also has four carbons. 'Butyrum' is Latin for butter.

name: 1,3-Butadiene
blurb: 4 carbons; two pairs hold hands twice (two double bonds).
facts: In World War II, Japan cut off most natural rubber. The US built a huge industry making synthetic rubber from butadiene.
It's also the 'B' in ABS, the tough plastic LEGO bricks are made from.

details.what: Four carbons with two double grips, one at each end. A gas used mainly to make rubber.
details.where: Car tires, hoses, shoe soles and the nitrile gloves used in clinics and kitchens.
details.bonds: Its two double grips sit on either side of a single one, so the electrons spread across all four carbons. Each molecule can link at both ends, giving bendy, stretchy rubber chains.
details.extra: Most of it comes as a side product when crackers make ethylene from heavier liquid feeds like naphtha. Ethane-fed crackers make very little.

name: Octane (iso-octane)
blurb: 8 carbons in a branched shape. Branching resists engine knock, which is where the 'octane rating' comes from.

lens.nexus: Gasoline-size molecules (C5-C12) are part of what your plant's oil can be refined into.

facts: The octane scale runs from heptane (0) to iso-octane (100). A fuel rated 90 knocks like a mix of 90% iso-octane and 10% heptane.
Some fuels score above 100, like racing fuels and pure ethanol.

details.what: Eight carbons bunched into a branched shape, fully loaded with hydrogen. A clear liquid that acts like ideal gasoline.
details.where: You don't buy it pure. Refineries build branched molecules like it on purpose and blend them into premium gasoline.
details.bonds: The branches pull the molecule into a compact ball. Compact molecules resist breaking apart too early in a hot, squeezed engine, so they burn smoothly instead of knocking.
details.extra: Before branched fuels were common, refiners added a lead chemical to stop knock. The US ban on leaded gasoline for cars took effect on January 1, 1996.

rankWhy: The standard for gasoline. An octane rating compares fuel to it.

name: Dodecane (RP-1 stand-in)
blurb: 12 carbons holding hands in a line. Kerosene and RP-1 are mixes of molecules around this size.
uses: Jet fuel and rocket kerosene size.

lens.rocket: RP-1 is very pure kerosene, burned by Falcon 9's Merlin engines. Long chains can leave carbon gunk (coking) in engines. That's one reason Starship chose methane.
lens.nexus: Diesel- and kerosene-size chains (about C10-C20) cool into liquid oil at your plant.

facts: Twelve-carbon chains boil around 216 °C, far hotter than gasoline-size molecules.
Jet fuel and RP-1 are cousins. RP-1 is held to tighter limits on sulfur and ring-shaped molecules, which helps keep rocket engines clean.

details.what: Twelve carbons in a straight chain, every spare hand holding a hydrogen. A clear, oily liquid.
details.where: Kerosene lamps, space heaters and jet fuel are mixes of chains around this size. Labs use pure dodecane as a simple test fuel.
details.bonds: Long chains of single grips are floppy, like string. Long strings tangle and cling, so it's oilier and boils much hotter than gasoline.
details.extra: In the 1800s, kerosene lamps replaced whale oil as the common way to light homes.

name: Hexadecane (cetane)
blurb: 16 carbons holding hands in a line. It's the yardstick for how well diesel ignites (the cetane number).

lens.nexus: Middle of your oil range. Much longer chains (C20+) are wax.

facts: Diesel engines have no spark plugs. They squeeze air until it's hot enough to light the fuel by itself.
Rudolf Diesel showed an engine running on peanut oil at the 1900 Paris World's Fair.
Hexadecane turns solid at about 18 °C. Long waxy chains like it are why diesel can gel in winter.

details.what: Sixteen carbons in a straight chain. An oily liquid right in the middle of the diesel size range.
details.where: Diesel for trucks, trains, ships and backup generators is a mix of chains around this size.
details.bonds: Long, straight chains break apart easily under heat and pressure. So they light quickly in a diesel engine, the opposite of what gasoline needs.
details.extra: The bottom of the original cetane scale was 1-methylnaphthalene, a ring molecule that barely ignites. It was later swapped for a branched molecule called isocetane.

name: Benzene
blurb: Six carbons hold hands in a ring, each also holding one hydrogen. Each has one spare hand, shared around the whole ring. That makes it very stable.
uses: Starting point for styrene, nylon, plastics, dyes.

lens.nexus: In the reactor's heat, broken pieces can curl up into rings like this (aromatics). They are a step on the road to char.

facts: Michael Faraday discovered benzene in 1825, in oily leftovers from the gas used for lamps.
August Kekulé said the ring shape came to him in a daydream of a snake biting its own tail.
Benzene can cause cancer, so it's kept to tiny amounts in gasoline.

details.what: Six carbons in a flat ring, each holding one hydrogen. A clear liquid with a sweet smell.
details.where: Small amounts are in crude oil, gasoline and cigarette smoke. Factories turn it into styrene, nylon and detergents.
details.bonds: The shared electrons spread evenly around the ring, so all six links are the same length. That even sharing makes the ring hard to break open, so benzene swaps its hydrogens instead.
details.extra: The first commercial decaf coffee, from about 1905, used benzene to wash out the caffeine. It was dropped once benzene was found to cause cancer.

rankWhy: Starting ring for nylon, polystyrene, dyes and many medicines.

name: Toluene
blurb: A benzene ring holding a methyl (CH3) group.
facts: TNT is toluene with three nitro groups added. Its full name is trinitrotoluene.
It was first found in tolu balsam, a South American tree sap, which gave it its name.

details.what: A benzene ring with a CH3 (methyl) group stuck on. A clear liquid that smells like paint thinner.
details.where: Paint thinner, nail polish, glues and gasoline.
details.bonds: The ring keeps its evenly shared electrons. The CH3 pushes a little extra electron charge into the ring, so toluene reacts a bit more easily than benzene.
details.extra: It does many of benzene's jobs as a solvent but is much less harmful. So it replaced benzene in many products.

name: Styrene
blurb: Benzene ring plus a C=C (vinyl) handle for linking up.
uses: Building block of polystyrene and ABS.

lens.nexus: Heated, polystyrene mostly unzips back to styrene, like a zipper. Polyethylene instead snaps at random spots.

facts: Tiny natural amounts of styrene show up in foods like cinnamon, strawberries and coffee.
It also goes into SBR, a synthetic rubber used in many car tires.

details.what: A benzene ring with a double-gripped CH=CH2 handle. A clear, oily liquid with a sweet smell.
details.where: Foam cups, fridge liners and the resin in fiberglass boats and bathtubs.
details.bonds: The double grip sits right next to the ring, and they share electrons a little. That makes the handle open easily, so styrene can link into chains just from warmth.
details.extra: Because it links up on its own, stored styrene needs a small added chemical that keeps it from turning solid in the tank.

name: Naphthalene
blurb: Two benzene rings joined at an edge. As more rings join, hydrogen per carbon drops toward zero.
uses: Mothballs, a starting point for dyes.

lens.nexus: Joined rings are how char grows. Keep stripping hydrogen and joining rings, and you head toward graphite-like carbon.

facts: Mothballs slowly turn from solid straight into gas. Those fumes are what keep moths away.
It was one of the first chemicals pulled out of coal tar, back in the early 1800s.

details.what: Two benzene rings sharing one edge. A white solid with a strong mothball smell.
details.where: Old-style mothballs, coal tar and car exhaust. Factories use it to make dyes and plastic softeners.
details.bonds: The shared electrons spread over both rings. Flat molecules stack neatly like plates, so it's a solid at room temperature even though it's small.
details.extra: Formosan subterranean termites fill their nests with naphthalene. Scientists think it helps keep out germs and invaders, just like a mothball.

name: Polyethylene
blurb: Ethylene lets go of its second grip. Each carbon uses that freed hand to grab the next one, over and over. Shown: a 6-carbon slice of a chain thousands of carbons long.
uses: Bags, films, bottles, pipe. The most common plastic.

lens.nexus: Your plant's main feed. Heat breaks the carbon-carbon grips (weaker than carbon-hydrogen) at random spots. That gives gas, oil, wax and char.

facts: It was discovered by accident in 1933 at the British company ICI, when a high-pressure test left a waxy white solid.
In World War II it insulated radar cables. That made radar light enough to fit in airplanes.

details.what: One carbon chain thousands of atoms long, wrapped in hydrogens. Soft, waxy and cheap.
details.where: Grocery bags, milk jugs, cling wrap, squeeze bottles and the plastic gas pipe under streets.
details.bonds: Inside a chain, the grips are strong. Between chains there's only weak cling, so heat lets chains slide and the plastic melts. Straight chains pack tight into stiff HDPE (high-density); branched chains give soft LDPE (low-density).
details.extra: Made with extra-long chains and stretched into fibers, the same plastic is strong enough for body armor and ship ropes.

rankWhy: The most common plastic: bags, bottles, films and pipes.

name: Polypropylene
blurb: Polyethylene's chain, with a CH3 branch on every other carbon.

lens.nexus: Breaks apart a bit more easily than polyethylene, because the branch points are weak spots.

facts: It can bend thousands of times without snapping, so it's used for 'living hinges' like flip-top bottle caps.
Australia made the first plastic banknotes in 1988, printed on polypropylene film.
Giulio Natta, who figured out how to make it in a neat, orderly form, shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

details.what: A long carbon chain with a CH3 branch on every other carbon. A tough, light plastic.
details.where: Yogurt cups, bottle caps, car bumpers, carpet, and the filter layer in face masks.
details.bonds: How the branches line up matters. When they all point the same way, chains pack into a stiff plastic that melts high. When they point randomly, you get a soft, sticky goo.
details.extra: Polypropylene and polyethylene are lighter than water, so they float. PET and PVC sink, which helps recyclers sort plastics in water tanks.

rankWhy: Second most common plastic: food tubs, car parts, bottle caps.

name: Polystyrene
blurb: A chain of carbons holding hands, with a benzene ring hanging off every other carbon.
facts: Foam polystyrene is about 98% air. That trapped air is why a foam cup keeps coffee hot.
The real 'Styrofoam' brand is blue building insulation. White foam cups are a different product people call by the same name.

details.what: A carbon chain with a benzene ring hanging off every other carbon. A hard, clear plastic, or a light foam when puffed with gas.
details.where: Foam cups, packing peanuts, egg cartons, disposable cutlery and yogurt cups.
details.bonds: The bulky rings keep chains from packing neatly. So solid polystyrene is glassy and clear, but brittle. It cracks instead of bending.
details.extra: Without the foam, polystyrene is clear as glass. Lab petri dishes and old CD cases are made from it.

name: PVC
blurb: Polyethylene, but every other carbon holds a chlorine in one hand instead of a hydrogen.

lens.nexus: A problem for your plant. Heating it releases HCl, which eats away equipment. It must be kept out of the feed.

facts: By weight, PVC is more than half chlorine.
PVC was stiff and brittle at first. In 1926 Waldo Semon at B.F. Goodrich found how to make it soft and bendy.
That soft PVC shows up in garden hoses, shower curtains and fake leather.

details.what: A carbon chain where every other carbon holds a chlorine. A tough, cheap plastic that shrugs off water and rot.
details.where: White plumbing pipe, vinyl siding, window frames, wire coatings and credit cards.
details.bonds: Chlorine pulls electrons toward itself, leaving slightly charged spots along each chain. Chains cling to each other more, so PVC is stiff unless softeners (plasticizers) are mixed in.
details.extra: The chlorine makes PVC hard to burn. It tends to put itself out once the flame is taken away.

rankWhy: Pipes, window frames, flooring and cable coating.

name: PTFE (Teflon)
blurb: Every hydrogen is swapped for fluorine. Carbon and fluorine grip harder than almost any one-hand hold. So almost nothing sticks or reacts.
uses: Non-stick coatings, seals, liners that resist chemicals.

lens.rocket: Used for seals and liners that must survive liquid oxygen.

facts: Roy Plunkett found it by accident in 1938. A gas tank seemed empty, and inside was a slippery white powder.
It helped build the first atomic bombs, because it could survive the harsh uranium gas used to enrich uranium.
Even geckos can't stick to it.

details.what: A carbon chain completely wrapped in fluorine atoms. A slippery, white plastic.
details.where: Non-stick pans, plumber's tape, waterproof breathable jackets like Gore-Tex, and wire coatings in aircraft.
details.bonds: Fluorines pack tightly around the chain like armor, and the chain twists into a slow spiral so they fit. They hold their electrons so tightly that other molecules find nothing to cling to.
details.extra: PTFE doesn't truly melt into a runny liquid. It only turns gel-like, so parts are made by pressing powder and baking it.

name: PET
blurb: Rings and ester links (C-O-C=O) in the chain. Those oxygens make it act very differently from polyethylene.

lens.nexus: Usually unwanted at your plant. Its oxygen ends up as CO2, water and acids instead of oil.

facts: Nathaniel Wyeth patented the PET soda bottle in 1973. His brother was the famous painter Andrew Wyeth.
The same plastic in a water bottle can be spun into fleece jackets and carpet.

details.what: A chain of flat rings linked by oxygen-containing joints called esters. A clear, strong plastic.
details.where: Soda and water bottles, food trays and the polyester in shirts.
details.bonds: The flat rings stack, and the oxygen joints add extra cling between chains. That makes PET stiff enough to hold fizzy pressure. But water can slowly cut those ester joints.
details.extra: PET is recycling code 1 and one of the most recycled plastics. Old bottles often come back as new bottles or as fiber.

rankWhy: Water and soda bottles, and polyester clothing.

name: Water
blurb: Oxygen has 2 hands, and each holds a hydrogen. Oxygen also keeps two pairs of electrons to itself. They push the H's into a bent shape.

lens.rocket: The main thing coming out of hydrogen and methane engines.
lens.nexus: Wet feed at your plant steals heat and adds oxygen to the products.

facts: Water expands about 9% when it freezes, so ice floats. Most solids sink in their own liquid.
Water is heaviest at about 4 °C, so lakes freeze from the top down and fish survive underneath.
The space station recycles about 98% of its water, including astronaut sweat and urine.

details.what: One oxygen holding two hydrogens in a bent shape. The only common substance we see as solid, liquid and gas in everyday life.
details.where: Oceans, clouds, ice caps, and more than half of your own body.
details.bonds: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so its end is slightly negative and the hydrogens slightly positive. Those ends stick to neighbors, called hydrogen bonds. Without them, a molecule this small would be a gas at room temperature.
details.extra: Water dissolves more kinds of things than almost any other liquid. That's why chemists call it the universal solvent.

rankWhy: Every living thing runs on it, and it covers most of the planet.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
blurb: Two oxygens hold hands, and that O-O grip is weak. It snaps easily, giving off oxygen and heat.
uses: Bleaching, killing germs, single-ingredient rocket fuel (high-test peroxide).

lens.rocket: High-test peroxide breaks down over silver, a catalyst (a helper that isn't used up), into hot steam and oxygen. Used in early rockets and thrusters.

facts: The bombardier beetle mixes hydrogen peroxide with other chemicals to shoot a boiling-hot spray at attackers.
The 1960s Bell Rocket Belt jetpack ran on hydrogen peroxide. It could only fly for about 20 seconds.
Drugstore peroxide is about 3%. Rocket-grade peroxide is often around 90%.

details.what: Water with one extra oxygen: H-O-O-H. It looks like water, but it's a strong bleach when concentrated.
details.where: The brown drugstore bottle, hair bleach, teeth whiteners and paper mills.
details.bonds: Light, heat and metals all help snap the weak O-O grip. That's why it's sold in brown bottles that block light.
details.extra: Your own cells make small amounts. An enzyme in your body called catalase breaks it down fast, which is why it foams on a cut.

rankWhy: Bleaches paper and cleans cuts. Breaks down into just water and oxygen.

name: Carbon monoxide
blurb: Carbon and oxygen hold hands three times: a very strong triple bond. It forms when there isn't enough oxygen to make CO2.
uses: Syngas (a gas mix for making chemicals and methanol); poisonous.
facts: It has no color, smell or taste. That's why homes need CO alarms.
Your blood grabs carbon monoxide about 200 times more tightly than oxygen. So even a little crowds out the oxygen.
In a blast furnace, CO is what pulls the oxygen off iron ore to leave iron.

details.what: One carbon and one oxygen gripped very tightly. A small, poisonous gas.
details.where: Car exhaust, furnaces, grills and wood stoves when they burn without enough air. Factories also make it on purpose to build other chemicals.
details.bonds: Its triple grip is one of the strongest known. Carbon also keeps a spare pair of electrons, which it uses to latch onto metals, like the iron in your blood.
details.extra: Mixed with hydrogen as 'syngas,' CO can be rebuilt into liquid fuel. Germany did this on a large scale in World War II using the Fischer-Tropsch process.

rankWhy: Poison gas from bad burning. Industry uses it to make steel and chemicals.

name: Carbon dioxide
blurb: Each oxygen has 2 hands and holds both with carbon. Two double grips use all 4 of carbon's hands.
uses: Fizzy drinks, dry ice, plant food; main greenhouse gas.

lens.rocket: Mars' air is about 95% CO2. That's the carbon source for making methane there.

facts: Dry ice is frozen CO2 at -78.5 °C. It turns straight into gas without melting first.
Mars has polar caps topped with frozen CO2 that grow and shrink with the seasons.
Warm soda goes flat faster because warm water holds less dissolved gas.

details.what: One carbon holding two oxygens in a straight line. The colorless gas we breathe out.
details.where: Your breath, soda fizz, fire extinguishers, and the air, where it's about 0.04% but matters a lot.
details.bonds: The molecule is straight and even, so its pulls cancel out. But it can bend and stretch, and that wobbling soaks up heat rays (infrared). That's how it traps heat in the air.
details.extra: Plants pull CO2 from the air and use sunlight to turn it into sugar. Nearly all the carbon in your body started out as CO2 that way.

rankWhy: What breathing and burning give off, what plants eat, and the main gas behind climate change.

name: Methanol
blurb: Methane, but one of carbon's hands holds an OH group instead of a hydrogen.
facts: It's called wood alcohol because it was first made by heating wood without air. That's pyrolysis, the same basic idea your plant uses on plastic.
It burns with a nearly invisible flame in daylight. Indy cars ran on it for years, which made pit fires hard to see.
Drinking even a small amount can cause blindness.

details.what: The simplest alcohol: one carbon holding three hydrogens and an OH group. A clear liquid that looks like water but is poisonous.
details.where: Windshield washer fluid, camp stove fuel, and a raw material for glues and plastics.
details.bonds: The OH end lets methanol molecules stick to each other and to water, like water does. That's why it mixes with water completely and boils far hotter than methane.
details.extra: Today it's made mostly from natural gas or coal, turned first into syngas. Some new cargo ships are built to burn methanol as a cleaner fuel.

rankWhy: A basic building block for plastics, glues and fuels.

name: Ethanol
blurb: Ethane, but one end holds an OH instead of a hydrogen.
facts: Yeast makes ethanol by eating sugar. Beer, wine and corn fuel ethanol all come from that same process.
Most US gasoline has about 10% ethanol mixed in, labeled E10.
Henry Ford's Model T could run on ethanol as well as gasoline.

details.what: Two carbons with an OH group on one end. The alcohol in drinks, and a clean-burning fuel.
details.where: Beer, wine, hand sanitizer, vanilla extract and most gas pumps.
details.bonds: Its OH end sticks to water, and its carbon end mixes with oils. That two-sided nature lets it dissolve both, which is why it's used for extracts and sanitizers.
details.extra: The CDC says hand sanitizer should be at least 60% alcohol to kill germs well.

rankWhy: In every alcoholic drink and blended into gasoline as fuel.

name: Dimethyl ether
blurb: Same atoms as ethanol, but oxygen sits in the middle: an isomer.
facts: DME boils at about -24 °C, while ethanol, with the very same atoms, boils at 78 °C.
Moving the oxygen to the middle removes the OH 'sticky end' that makes ethanol molecules cling to each other.

details.what: Two CH3 groups joined through one oxygen. A gas at room temperature, with the same atoms as ethanol.
details.where: Spray cans, and test trucks that run on it in place of diesel.
details.bonds: There's no carbon-carbon grip anywhere in it. With nothing to build soot from, it burns with almost no smoke.
details.extra: It's the simplest ether. Its bigger cousin, diethyl ether, was one of the first surgical anesthetics, starting in the 1840s.

name: Formaldehyde
blurb: Carbon holds oxygen with 2 hands and a hydrogen in each other hand.
facts: Your own body makes small amounts of formaldehyde as part of normal chemistry.
That new-furniture smell can include formaldehyde slowly leaking from glues in pressed wood.

details.what: The simplest molecule with a C=O end: one carbon holding an oxygen with two hands and two hydrogens. A sharp-smelling gas.
details.where: Glues in plywood and particleboard, some wrinkle-free fabrics, and vaccines, where it's used to make germs or toxins harmless.
details.bonds: Oxygen pulls the double grip toward itself, leaving the carbon a little positive. That carbon grabs other molecules, so formaldehyde links things together easily. That's why it makes strong glues.
details.extra: In 1969 it became the first many-atom carbon molecule found in the clouds between stars.

name: Acetic acid
blurb: A methyl (CH3) group holding hands with a carboxylic acid (COOH) group.
uses: Vinegar, making PET and vinyl acetate.
facts: Vinegar is mostly water with about 4 to 8% acetic acid.
Pure acetic acid freezes at about 17 °C, a cool room. The icy-looking crystals are why it's called 'glacial' acetic acid.

details.what: Two carbons where one end is an acid group (COOH). The sour taste in vinegar.
details.where: Vinegar, ketchup, pickles, and the vinegar smell of some silicone caulks while they set.
details.bonds: The OH on the acid end lets go of its hydrogen in water. That loose hydrogen is what tastes sour and what dissolves crusty mineral buildup.
details.extra: Most factory acetic acid is made by joining methanol with carbon monoxide over a metal catalyst (a helper that isn't used up).

rankWhy: Vinegar, and a building block for PET plastic and paints.

name: Acetone
blurb: A C=O carbon holding a methyl group on each side.
facts: Your body makes acetone when it burns fat for fuel, like during fasting. It can show up on your breath.
In World War I, Chaim Weizmann found a way to make acetone with bacteria, which Britain needed for explosives. He later became Israel's first president.

details.what: Three carbons, with an oxygen held by two hands on the middle carbon. A clear liquid that evaporates fast.
details.where: Hardware store solvents, superglue remover and lab cleaning.
details.bonds: The C=O end is slightly charged, so it mixes with water. The two CH3 ends dissolve oils, paints and plastics. Molecules cling only weakly, so it evaporates quickly and feels cold on skin.
details.extra: It dissolves foam polystyrene so well that a foam cup collapses into a small, sticky blob.

name: Ethylene glycol
blurb: Ethane, but each end holds an OH instead of a hydrogen.
facts: It tastes sweet but is poisonous. Many antifreeze brands now add a bitter chemical so pets and kids won't drink it.
A 50/50 mix with water won't freeze until about -37 °C.

details.what: Two carbons with an OH group on each end. A thick, sweet, poisonous liquid.
details.where: Car coolant, airplane de-icing fluid and PET bottles.
details.bonds: Its two OH ends grip water at both ends. That gets in the way of water lining up into ice, so the mix freezes much colder. It also boils hotter than water, so coolant handles summer heat.
details.extra: In PET, each of glycol's two OH ends grabs an acid. That links piece after piece into a long plastic chain.

name: Glucose
blurb: A ring of 5 carbons and 1 oxygen, with OH groups all around.
uses: Blood sugar; building block of starch and cellulose.
facts: Your brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your energy, mostly from glucose.
Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. A small change in how the links point is why you can digest bread but not wood.

details.what: A ring of five carbons and one oxygen, with OH groups around it. The sugar your body runs on.
details.where: Blood, fruit, honey and corn syrup. Plants make it from sunlight, water and CO2.
details.bonds: All those OH groups stick to water, so glucose dissolves easily. Your cells break its grips one step at a time, releasing energy slowly instead of as a flame.
details.extra: Blood sugar meters for diabetes measure glucose in one drop of blood. A test strip uses an enzyme that reacts only with glucose.

rankWhy: The sugar every cell burns for energy. Plants make it from sunlight.

name: Ammonia
blurb: Nitrogen has 3 hands, each holding a hydrogen. It keeps one pair of electrons to itself, on top.
facts: Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch learned to make ammonia from air in the early 1900s. Fertilizer from their process helps feed about half the people on Earth.
Roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through an ammonia factory first.
The X-15 rocket plane burned ammonia with liquid oxygen.

details.what: One nitrogen holding three hydrogens, shaped like a short pyramid. A gas with a sharp smell that stings the eyes.
details.where: Window cleaners, farm fertilizer and smelling salts.
details.bonds: Nitrogen's spare pair of electrons on top can grab a hydrogen ion (H+), turning it into ammonium (NH4+). That's why ammonia is a base, the opposite of an acid.
details.extra: Ammonia holds lots of hydrogen and no carbon. Engineers are testing it as a carbon-free fuel for large ships.

rankWhy: Made from air and natural gas. Fertilizer from it helps feed a large share of humanity.

name: Hydrogen cyanide
blurb: Carbon holds nitrogen with 3 hands (a triple bond) and a hydrogen with its 4th.
uses: Starting point for nylon and acrylic; very poisonous.
facts: Cyanide smells like bitter almonds to some people. Many others can't smell it at all because of their genes.
Apple seeds and peach pits hold a chemical that can release small amounts of HCN when chewed.

details.what: A hydrogen, a carbon and a nitrogen in a straight line. A very poisonous liquid that boils at about 26 °C, just above room temperature.
details.where: Factories that make nylon and acrylic. Small amounts form when plastics and wool burn.
details.bonds: The C≡N triple grip forms cyanide. Cyanide latches onto a key enzyme cells use to burn oxygen, so cells suffocate even with oxygen around.
details.extra: Cyanide made from HCN is used to pull gold and silver out of crushed rock. It grabs the metal atoms and carries them into water.

name: Nitrous oxide
blurb: A straight N-N-O chain with charge spread across it.
uses: Anesthetic, whipped cream propellant, oxygen source for hybrid rockets.

lens.rocket: The oxygen source in hybrid rocket motors. It builds its own tank pressure.

facts: In 1799 Humphry Davy tested laughing gas on himself and his friends. It later became one of the first anesthetics.
Under pressure it dissolves into cream's fat. When sprayed out, it puffs up and makes the cream fluffy.

details.what: Two nitrogens and an oxygen in a line. A sweet-smelling gas called laughing gas.
details.where: Dentist offices, whipped cream cans and racing cars. Fertilized soil also gives it off.
details.bonds: The molecule holds its oxygen loosely. Heated, it breaks apart and releases that oxygen, which lets engines burn extra fuel.
details.extra: A 2009 study found it's now the biggest human-made threat to the ozone layer. It's also a strong greenhouse gas.

name: Nitrogen dioxide
blurb: An odd number of electrons, so one hand is always left empty. That makes it a reactive radical.
uses: Part of smog; making nitric acid.
facts: NO2 is the brown haze in smoggy city air.
Car engines make it by accident. The heat is so high that nitrogen and oxygen from the air join up.
Catalytic converters exist partly to turn it back into harmless nitrogen.

details.what: One nitrogen holding two oxygens, with one electron left unpaired. A reddish-brown, sharp-smelling gas.
details.where: Car and truck exhaust, power plants and gas stoves in homes.
details.bonds: The unpaired electron is an empty hand looking for a partner. In sunlight NO2 breaks apart, and the loose oxygen helps make ground-level ozone.
details.extra: Lightning makes nitrogen oxides like this naturally. Rain carries them down to soil as a natural fertilizer.

name: Dinitrogen tetroxide
blurb: Two NO2 molecules each have one empty hand. They grab each other, making an N-N bond.
uses: Rocket oxygen source that stores well.

lens.rocket: With hydrazine fuels it catches fire on contact (hypergolic), so no igniter is needed. Used on Dragon's Draco thrusters.

facts: N2O4 and NO2 keep switching back and forth. Cold favors colorless N2O4, and warmth turns it into brown NO2.
The Apollo service module engine burned it with a hydrazine fuel blend. Since it lit on contact, there was no igniter to fail.

details.what: Two NO2 molecules joined by an N-N grip. A liquid that supplies oxygen for burning.
details.where: Spacecraft and missile tanks. It's rarely seen outside aerospace and chemical plants.
details.bonds: The link joining the two halves is much weaker than the grips inside each half. So it splits easily, and its many oxygens are easy to hand over.
details.extra: The Titan II rockets that flew NASA's Gemini astronauts burned N2O4 with a hydrazine fuel. As missiles, they could sit fully fueled for long stretches.

name: Hydrazine
blurb: Two nitrogens hold hands. Each uses its other 2 hands to hold hydrogens.
uses: Single-ingredient satellite thruster fuel, foaming agents.

lens.rocket: Breaks down into hot gas over iridium, a catalyst (a helper that isn't used up). The classic satellite thruster fuel.

facts: The Voyager probes use hydrazine thrusters to keep their antennas pointed at Earth. In 2017, engineers fired Voyager 1 backup thrusters that had sat unused for 37 years.
It's so toxic that crews fueling spacecraft wear full protective suits.

details.what: Two nitrogens holding hands, each also holding two hydrogens. A clear, fuming, toxic liquid.
details.where: Satellite thrusters and power plant boilers, where a little of it strips oxygen out of the water to stop rust.
details.bonds: The N-N grip is weak. Breaking it frees the nitrogens to form N2's super-strong triple grip. That swap releases a lot of energy, so hydrazine breaks down hot and fast.
details.extra: The F-16 fighter jet carries hydrazine to run its emergency power unit if the main engine quits.

name: Monomethylhydrazine
blurb: Hydrazine, but one hand holds a methyl (CH3) group instead of a hydrogen.
uses: Storable rocket fuel that lights on contact.

lens.rocket: Paired with N2O4 in spacecraft thrusters such as Dragon's Draco and SuperDraco.

facts: The Space Shuttle's orbital maneuvering engines burned MMH with N2O4.
Plain hydrazine freezes at about 2 °C. Adding the methyl group drops that to about -52 °C, handy in cold space.

details.what: Hydrazine with one hydrogen swapped for a CH3 group. A clear, toxic liquid used as rocket fuel.
details.where: Almost only in spacecraft and the plants that make it: crew capsules, satellites and space probes.
details.bonds: It keeps hydrazine's weak N-N grip. The added carbon brings a little more energy when it burns with an oxygen supplier.
details.extra: NASA's Orion capsule rides on a European-built service module whose engines burn MMH.

name: Urea
blurb: A C=O carbon with two NH2 groups.
facts: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from non-living chemicals. That broke the old belief that only living things could make such compounds.
Your body makes urea to get rid of extra nitrogen. Its name comes from urine, where it leaves.
Diesel exhaust fluid is 32.5% urea in water. Sprayed into hot exhaust, it helps turn smog gases into plain nitrogen and water.

details.what: A carbon with an oxygen and two NH2 groups. White crystals that dissolve easily in water.
details.where: Fertilizer pellets, diesel exhaust fluid, skin creams and the glues in particleboard.
details.bonds: Its N-H and C=O parts both stick to water, so it dissolves very easily. Nearly half its weight is nitrogen, which makes it a compact fertilizer.
details.extra: Urea is made from ammonia and CO2. So urea plants usually sit right next to ammonia plants, using their CO2 by-product.

rankWhy: The world's most-used nitrogen fertilizer. Your body makes it too.

name: Nitric acid
blurb: Nitrogen holds three oxygens. One of them also holds the hydrogen.
facts: Mixed with hydrochloric acid, it makes aqua regia, one of the few liquids that dissolves gold.
In 1940 a chemist hid two gold Nobel medals from the Nazis by dissolving them in aqua regia. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals were recast.
Most of it is made by burning ammonia over a platinum mesh.

details.what: One nitrogen holding three oxygens, one of which also holds a hydrogen. A strong, corrosive acid.
details.where: Fertilizer plants, explosives factories, and jewelers testing whether gold is real.
details.bonds: The nitrogen pulls hard on its oxygens, so the hydrogen comes off easily in water: a strong acid. It also hands out oxygen readily, which is why it eats metals like copper.
details.extra: A drop on skin turns it yellow, because nitric acid reacts with the proteins in skin.

rankWhy: Turns ammonia into fertilizer and explosives.

name: Hydrogen sulfide
blurb: Sulfur, like oxygen, has 2 hands. Each holds a hydrogen.
uses: Rotten-egg gas in sour crude and natural gas; where refinery sulfur comes from.

lens.nexus: Sulfur in your plant's feed ends up as H2S and other sulfur chemicals. They must be scrubbed out of the gas and oil.

facts: You can smell tiny traces of it, but high levels knock out your sense of smell. So a smell that fades can mean danger.
Rotten eggs smell this way because bacteria break down the sulfur in egg proteins.

details.what: One sulfur holding two hydrogens, bent like water. A toxic gas that smells like rotten eggs.
details.where: Sewers, swamps, hot springs, and 'sour' oil and gas wells.
details.bonds: Sulfur pulls on electrons much less than oxygen does. So H2S molecules barely stick to each other, and it's a gas while water is a liquid.
details.extra: Refineries turn H2S into yellow sulfur using the Claus process. Most of the world's sulfur now comes from cleaning oil and gas this way.

name: Sulfur dioxide
blurb: Sulfur is bigger, so it can hold out extra hands. It holds each oxygen with 2 hands.
uses: Making sulfuric acid, keeping food fresh; a cause of acid rain.
facts: After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, its sulfur dioxide cooled the whole planet by about 0.5 °C for a while.
The sharp smell of a just-struck match is partly sulfur dioxide.

details.what: One sulfur holding two oxygens in a bent shape. A choking gas with a sharp, burnt smell.
details.where: Volcanoes and coal power plants. Small amounts keep wine and dried fruit fresh, listed as 'sulfites.'
details.bonds: Sulfur can hold out more hands, so SO2 happily grabs another oxygen and becomes SO3. In damp air that turns into sulfuric acid, which falls as acid rain.
details.extra: Power plant scrubbers spray a limestone slurry to catch SO2. The leftover is gypsum, which is used to make drywall.

name: Sulfuric acid
blurb: Sulfur in the middle holds four oxygens. Two of them also hold a hydrogen.
uses: The most-made industrial chemical: fertilizer, batteries, refining.
facts: A country's sulfuric acid output was once used as a measure of how industrial it was.
It pulls water out of sugar so hard that the sugar turns into a tall, steaming column of black carbon.
The clouds of Venus are made of sulfuric acid droplets.

details.what: One sulfur holding four oxygens, two of which hold hydrogens. A thick, oily, very strong acid.
details.where: Car batteries, some drain cleaners, fertilizer plants and refineries.
details.bonds: Its hydrogens come off easily in water. It also grabs water greedily and gives off a lot of heat doing it. That's why you always add acid to water, never water to acid.
details.extra: Its old name was 'oil of vitriol,' from its oily look and the glassy crystals it was first made from.

rankWhy: Made in larger amounts than almost any other chemical. Used for fertilizer, metals and batteries.

name: Hydrogen chloride
blurb: 1 hand each, so they hold hands once. In water it becomes hydrochloric acid.

lens.nexus: Given off when PVC is heated. That's why PVC is screened out of your plant's feed.

facts: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid. Stomach juice has a pH around 1.5 to 3.5.
A thick layer of mucus keeps that acid from eating your stomach wall.

details.what: One hydrogen holding one chlorine. A gas with a stinging smell that fumes in damp air.
details.where: Your stomach, pool chemicals that lower pH, and brick and concrete cleaners.
details.bonds: Chlorine pulls the shared pair hard, so in water the hydrogen walks off as H+. Almost every molecule splits this way, which makes it a strong acid.
details.extra: Hardware stores sell it as 'muriatic acid,' an old name from the Latin word for brine.

rankWhy: Your stomach acid. Industry uses it to clean steel and make PVC.

name: Hydrogen fluoride
blurb: They hold hands once, but fluorine tugs the handshake hard toward itself.
uses: Etching glass, alkylation in refineries, fluorine chemicals.

lens.nexus: Some refineries use HF as the catalyst (helper) in alkylation, a step that builds high-octane gasoline.

facts: HF is called a 'weak' acid, but it's one of the most dangerous. It slips through skin and pulls calcium out of the body.
Almost all fluorine chemicals, from Teflon to refrigerants, start out as HF.

details.what: One hydrogen holding one fluorine. A fuming liquid or gas, and a very dangerous acid in water.
details.where: Chip factories, some refineries, and a few heavy-duty rust stain removers.
details.bonds: Fluorine pulls the pair so hard that HF molecules stick strongly to each other. So it boils near room temperature, far hotter than HCl.
details.extra: The standard first aid for HF burns is calcium gluconate gel. It gives the fluoride calcium to grab before it takes calcium from the body.

name: Carbon tetrachloride
blurb: Methane's shape, but carbon's 4 hands hold chlorines instead of hydrogens.
uses: Once a solvent and used to make refrigerants; now restricted.
facts: It was once used in fire extinguishers. But on hot surfaces it can form phosgene, a poison gas, so it was dropped.
It also harms the ozone layer, so it's controlled by the Montreal Protocol treaty.

details.what: One carbon holding four chlorines. A heavy, clear liquid that doesn't burn.
details.where: Rarely seen now outside labs. It was once common in dry cleaning and spot removers.
details.bonds: The four chlorines spread evenly around carbon, so their pulls cancel and the molecule isn't lopsided. That's why it dissolves grease and oils but not water.
details.extra: Early lava lamps used it to make the wax heavier. A US ban on it in consumer products took effect in 1970.

name: Tetrafluoromethane
blurb: Carbon's 4 hands each hold a fluorine. Extremely stable.
facts: CF4 is one of the longest-lasting gases known. Once released, it stays in the air for about 50,000 years.
Aluminum smelters give off small amounts of CF4 as a by-product.

details.what: One carbon holding four fluorines. A colorless, odorless gas that hardly reacts with anything.
details.where: Mostly inside chip factories. Tiny amounts float in the air from aluminum smelting.
details.bonds: Carbon-fluorine grips are among the strongest single bonds. With fluorines covering all four sides, there's no weak spot to attack.
details.extra: It's also a refrigerant, called R-14, used for very low-temperature cooling.

name: Chloroform
blurb: Carbon's 4 hands hold one hydrogen and three chlorines.
facts: In 1853 Dr. John Snow gave Queen Victoria chloroform while she gave birth. That made pain relief in childbirth popular.
Movies show it knocking someone out in seconds. In real life it takes minutes and can easily kill.

details.what: One carbon holding one hydrogen and three chlorines. A heavy, sweet-smelling liquid.
details.where: Chemistry labs, where it dissolves fats and oils. Tiny amounts form in chlorinated tap water.
details.bonds: The three chlorines pull electrons away from carbon, which makes the last hydrogen slightly positive. That lets chloroform cling a little to other molecules, helping it dissolve many things.
details.extra: Light and air slowly turn it into phosgene, a poison gas. So it's stored in brown bottles with a little ethanol added.

name: Phosphine
blurb: Phosphorus, like nitrogen, has 3 hands. Each holds a hydrogen.
facts: In 2020 scientists reported possible signs of phosphine in Venus's clouds. The finding is still being debated.
Impure phosphine smells like garlic or rotting fish.

details.what: One phosphorus holding three hydrogens, shaped like ammonia. A toxic, flammable gas.
details.where: Grain silo fumigation and chip factories. Rotting matter in swamps makes tiny amounts.
details.bonds: Phosphorus is bigger than nitrogen, so its grips on hydrogen are weaker and its pyramid is squeezed narrower. Unlike ammonia, it barely acts as a base.
details.extra: One old idea for the ghostly lights over marshes, called will-o'-the-wisps, is phosphine setting swamp methane alight.

name: Phosphorus trichloride
blurb: Phosphorus's 3 hands each hold a chlorine.
facts: It reacts with water so fast that it fumes in damp air, giving off HCl.
Phosphorus has 3 hands like nitrogen, so PCl3 is shaped like a short pyramid, just like ammonia.

details.what: One phosphorus holding three chlorines. A clear, fuming, toxic liquid.
details.where: Chemical plants that make weed killers like glyphosate, flame retardants and plastic additives.
details.bonds: Its grips on chlorine break easily when water comes along. Water swaps in for chlorine and releases HCl, so PCl3 must be kept bone-dry.
details.extra: French chemists Gay-Lussac and Thénard first made it in 1808. Humphry Davy made it the same year by burning phosphorus in chlorine.

name: Sulfur hexafluoride
blurb: Sulfur is big enough to hold out 6 hands, more than the usual rule. Extremely stable.
facts: SF6 is about 5 times heavier than air. Breathing it makes your voice sound very deep, the opposite of helium.
A foil boat can float on an invisible pool of SF6 gas in a fish tank.
It's the strongest greenhouse gas known, about 23,500 times stronger than CO2 pound for pound over 100 years.

details.what: One sulfur holding six fluorines, pointing out like a six-armed jack. A heavy gas with no color or smell.
details.where: Sealed inside high-voltage switches at power substations.
details.bonds: The six fluorines wrap sulfur completely, so nothing can reach it. It also soaks up stray electrons, which stops sparks from jumping inside electrical gear.
details.extra: From 1989 to 2006, Nike filled its Air shoe cushions with SF6, because its big molecules leak out slowly. Nike switched because SF6 is such a strong greenhouse gas.

name: Silane
blurb: Silicon sits below carbon, so it also has 4 hands, each holding a hydrogen: silicon's methane.
uses: Making ultra-pure silicon for chips and solar cells.
facts: Silane catches fire by itself in air, so a leak at a chip plant can burn with no spark at all.
Silicon can't build long, stable chains the way carbon can. That's one reason life is built on carbon.

details.what: One silicon holding four hydrogens: silicon's version of methane. A colorless gas.
details.where: Only in chip and solar panel factories, piped in to grow thin silicon layers.
details.bonds: Silicon is bigger than carbon and holds hydrogen less tightly. Those weaker grips break easily, which is why silane bursts into flame in air while methane needs a spark.
details.extra: Heated, it splits into silicon and hydrogen gas. That's how thin silicon films are laid down on solar cells and flat screens.

name: Triethylborane
blurb: Boron has only 3 hands, so it holds 3 groups. Even then it has a gap that wants electrons. That hunger is why it catches fire on contact with air.
uses: Igniter that catches fire by itself in air.

lens.rocket: The TEB in TEA-TEB, which lights Falcon 9's Merlin engines with a green flash.

facts: The SR-71 Blackbird spy plane also used TEB to light its engines. It carried only enough for a limited number of starts.
Boron is what gives TEB's flame its green color.

details.what: One boron holding three ethyl (C2H5) groups. A clear liquid that bursts into flame in air.
details.where: Rocket and jet engine igniters, and some chemistry labs.
details.bonds: Each boron-carbon grip is weak, while a boron-oxygen grip is very strong. Trading one for the other releases the heat that lights the flame.
details.extra: Chemists use a dash of TEB plus air to make radicals (pieces with an empty hand). Those start chain reactions for building medicines and plastics.

name: Triethylaluminium
blurb: Aluminum, like boron, holds with 3 hands but still has a gap that wants electrons. So it reacts violently with oxygen and water.

lens.rocket: The TEA in TEA-TEB igniter on Falcon 9.
lens.nexus: Teams up with titanium catalysts (Ziegler-Natta) to make polyethylene and polypropylene.

facts: Karl Ziegler's work with aluminum compounds like this earned him a share of the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Each Merlin engine relight uses up a shot of TEA-TEB, so the supply limits how many times it can restart.

details.what: One aluminum holding three ethyl groups. A clear liquid that bursts into flame in air and explodes with water.
details.where: Shipped in sealed steel cylinders to plastics plants and rocket launch sites.
details.bonds: Aluminum holds its carbon groups loosely and wants more electrons. So two molecules pair up, sharing groups as bridges between the aluminums. In the bottle it's really a double molecule.
details.extra: Its fires can't be put out with water or CO2. Crews use dry sand or special powders instead.

name: Xenon difluoride
blurb: Xenon has 0 hands. But it's big, with outer electrons far from its center, so fluorine can tug them into handshakes anyway.
uses: Adds fluorine to other chemicals; etching silicon.
facts: Before 1962, textbooks said noble gases could never form compounds. Neil Bartlett proved them wrong with xenon.
XeF2 is a stable solid that forms colorless crystals you can keep in a bottle.

details.what: One xenon atom with a fluorine on each side, in a straight line. Colorless crystals.
details.where: Research labs, and chip plants that carve tiny moving parts like the motion sensors in phones.
details.bonds: Xenon keeps three pairs of its own electrons around its middle. They push the two fluorines to opposite ends, making a straight line.
details.extra: Bartlett's first noble gas compound in 1962 was a xenon-platinum-fluorine solid. Simpler xenon fluorides like XeF2 followed that same year.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride
blurb: Four fluorines around xenon in a flat square.
uses: Proof that noble gases aren't totally inert.
facts: XeF4 was first made in 1962, the same year as Bartlett's discovery, by heating xenon with fluorine.
Xenon keeps two pairs of electrons to itself, one above and one below. They push the four fluorines into that flat square.

details.what: One xenon with four fluorines around it in a flat square. Colorless crystals.
details.where: Only in research labs. It's a chemistry curiosity, not an everyday material.
details.bonds: Its grips with fluorine are fragile compared with most bonds. Even moist air starts breaking it down, so it's kept bone-dry.
details.extra: Water turns part of it into xenon trioxide, a solid that can explode when dry.

name: Nickel carbonyl
blurb: Four CO molecules each give nickel both halves of a handshake. Very poisonous gas.
facts: Ludwig Mond discovered it around 1890. It was the first known compound of a metal bonded to carbon monoxide.
It boils at only 43 °C. So nickel can be carried off as a gas, then dropped back out as pure metal by heating.

details.what: One nickel atom with four CO molecules around it. A colorless, extremely toxic liquid that evaporates easily.
details.where: Only inside nickel refineries. The Clydach refinery in Wales has run on the Mond process since 1902.
details.bonds: Each CO hands nickel a pair of electrons, and nickel hands some back. This two-way sharing holds the molecule together, and gentle heat undoes it.
details.extra: It's far more dangerous than CO alone. Breathing small amounts can cause lung damage that shows up days later.

name: Ammonium perchlorate
blurb: A solid of charged pieces, NH4+ and ClO4-, stuck together like magnets. The ClO4- carries 4 oxygens ready to hand over.
uses: Oxygen source in solid rocket boosters (mixed with aluminum powder).

lens.rocket: Shuttle SRBs and SLS boosters burn ammonium perchlorate with aluminum powder in a rubbery binder.

facts: In 1988 a Nevada factory making ammonium perchlorate for the Space Shuttle blew up in a series of huge explosions.
NASA's Phoenix lander found perchlorates in Martian soil in 2008.

details.what: A white salt of ammonium (NH4+) and perchlorate (ClO4-) pieces. It packs something to burn and an oxygen supplier into one crystal.
details.where: Solid rocket motors, from high-power hobby rockets to missiles and space boosters, and some fireworks.
details.bonds: Inside each piece, atoms hold hands. Between pieces, opposite charges stick like magnets. The ClO4- holds its oxygens loosely enough to give them up in a fire.
details.extra: Most solid motors can't be shut off once lit. That's a big difference from liquid engines, which can be throttled and stopped.

name: Sodium chloride
blurb: Sodium would rather give away its 1 loose electron. Chlorine has 1 empty hand and takes it. Now Na+ and Cl- stick like magnets in a grid, not as molecules.
uses: Table salt; source of chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
facts: Sodium is a metal that bursts into flame in water, and chlorine is a poison gas. Together they make something you sprinkle on food.
Each grain of table salt is a tiny cube, because its grid of atoms is cube-shaped.

details.what: Table salt: a grid of sodium and chloride ions (charged atoms), alternating + and -.
details.where: Kitchen salt, seawater, road salt, and thick underground salt beds left by ancient seas.
details.bonds: Every + sits surrounded by six -, and every - by six +. The grip is strong but rigid, so a salt crystal is hard but shatters when hit instead of bending.
details.extra: About 3.5% of seawater's weight is dissolved salts, most of it sodium chloride.

rankWhy: Table salt. Your body needs it, and it's the starting point for chlorine and lye.

name: Potassium chloride
blurb: Same as table salt: one electron handed over.
facts: Bananas are rich in potassium, and a tiny share of all potassium is naturally radioactive.
'Potash' means pot ash. Early settlers made potassium salts by soaking wood ashes in pots.

details.what: A grid of potassium and chloride ions, built just like table salt.
details.where: Fertilizer bags, salt substitutes and water softener pellets.
details.bonds: Potassium is bigger than sodium, so its ions sit farther apart and the grid grips a bit less tightly. That's why KCl melts at a lower temperature than table salt.
details.extra: Saskatchewan, in western Canada, sits on the largest known potash deposits in the world.

rankWhy: Potash: the main way farms get potassium. Also a salt substitute.

name: Lithium fluoride
blurb: Lithium gives 1, fluorine takes 1.
facts: In the 1960s, Oak Ridge ran a test nuclear reactor using a melted salt made with lithium fluoride.
Unlike table salt, it barely dissolves in water.

details.what: A grid of lithium and fluoride ions. A clear, very stable crystal.
details.where: You won't find it at home. It's used in special optics, metal-joining fluxes and research reactors.
details.bonds: Both ions are tiny, so they sit very close and grip hard. That tight hold makes the crystal tough to break down and lets even deep ultraviolet light pass through.
details.extra: LiF chips in radiation badges store energy from radiation. Heated later, they glow, and the brightness tells the dose.

name: Magnesium oxide
blurb: Magnesium gives away 2 electrons; oxygen's 2 empty hands take them. Double charges grip hard, so it melts at about 2,800 °C.
facts: Burning magnesium ribbon makes a blinding white flash. The white ash left behind is MgO.
MgO bricks line steel furnaces that hold molten steel at over 1,500 °C.

details.what: A grid of magnesium and oxide ions. A white powder, or a very hard ceramic.
details.where: Furnace linings, fireproof building boards, and magnesium supplement pills.
details.bonds: Both ions carry a double charge, so they pull on each other much harder than the single charges in table salt. That's why it handles heat so well.
details.extra: Electric stove and oven heating elements are packed with MgO powder. It blocks electricity but lets heat pass through.

name: Calcium oxide
blurb: Calcium gives 2 electrons; oxygen takes 2.
facts: Heated in a hot flame, quicklime glows bright white. Old theaters used it for stage lights, which is where 'in the limelight' comes from.
Adding water to quicklime gives off enough heat to boil the water.
Cement plants make it by baking limestone, which releases CO2. That's a big part of cement's carbon footprint.

details.what: A grid of calcium and oxide ions. A white, crumbly solid called quicklime.
details.where: Cement, steel mills, paper mills and water treatment plants.
details.bonds: Double charges grip tightly, so it takes extreme heat to melt it. But it grabs water eagerly and turns into slaked lime (calcium hydroxide).
details.extra: Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash to make concrete that still stands today, like the dome of the Pantheon.

rankWhy: Lime: comes from limestone and goes into cement, steelmaking and water treatment.

name: Calcium fluoride
blurb: Calcium gives away 2 electrons, so it takes 2 fluorines (1 each).
facts: Fluorite gave its name to both fluorine and the word 'fluorescence,' because some pieces glow under UV light.
Its name comes from the Latin word 'to flow.' Metal workers added it to help melted metal and slag flow.

details.what: A grid with two fluoride ions for every calcium ion. The mineral fluorite.
details.where: Colorful fluorite crystals in rock shops, in purple, green and blue, and high-end camera and telescope lenses.
details.bonds: Calcium's double charge pulls in two fluorides. Small, tightly held ions make a clear crystal that lets ultraviolet and infrared light through.
details.extra: Fluorite is the 4 on the Mohs scratch-hardness scale used by rock collectors.

name: Magnesium chloride
blurb: Magnesium gives 2 electrons, so it pairs with 2 chlorines.
facts: The Dead Sea is unusually rich in magnesium chloride.
Tofu makers use it, called nigari in Japan, to curdle soy milk.

details.what: A grid of magnesium ions with two chloride ions each. White crystals that dissolve easily.
details.where: Dust control on dirt roads, bath flakes, and seawater.
details.bonds: Magnesium's small size and double charge hold water molecules tightly around it. So it pulls moisture from the air and gives off heat as it dissolves.
details.extra: In 1941 Dow began making magnesium from seawater in Freeport, Texas. The process turns it into magnesium chloride, then splits out the metal with electricity.

name: Calcium chloride
blurb: Calcium gives 2, each chlorine takes 1.
facts: Dissolving it in water gives off heat, which helps it melt ice even in deep cold.
It pulls so much water from the air that a pile left out can dissolve into a puddle by itself.

details.what: A grid of calcium ions with two chloride ions each. White flakes or pellets.
details.where: Ice-melt bags, moisture-soaking tubs in closets, and canned pickles and vegetables to keep them crisp.
details.bonds: Dissolved, each unit splits into three loose pieces: one calcium and two chlorides. More pieces get in the way of ice forming, so it melts ice at colder temperatures than table salt.
details.extra: Cheesemakers add a little to milk, especially store-bought milk, to help it set into firm curds.

name: Aluminum oxide
blurb: Aluminum gives away 3 electrons; oxygen takes 2. The smallest even match is 2 Al to 3 O (6 electrons each way).
uses: Sapphire, grinding grit, catalyst supports, the protective skin on aluminum.

lens.nexus: Alumina is a common base for catalysts (reaction helpers), and part of zeolite and clay catalysts.
lens.rocket: The white smoke from solid rocket boosters is mostly aluminum oxide particles.

facts: Rubies and sapphires are both aluminum oxide. A trace of chromium makes red ruby, and iron and titanium make blue sapphire.
Aluminum metal is made by pulling the oxygen off alumina using huge amounts of electricity.

details.what: A grid of aluminum and oxide ions, two aluminums for every three oxygens. A very hard white solid.
details.where: Sandpaper, knife sharpeners, spark plug insulators and scratch-proof watch faces.
details.bonds: Small, highly charged ions lock into a tight grid. That makes it a 9 on the Mohs hardness scale, second only to diamond among common minerals.
details.extra: In 1902 Auguste Verneuil announced a way to melt alumina powder in a flame and grow crystals. Lab-made rubies and sapphires have been around ever since.

rankWhy: The ore that aluminum metal is made from. Also sandpaper grit and sapphire.

name: Iron(III) oxide
blurb: Iron gives 3 electrons, oxygen takes 2, so 2 Fe balance 3 O. This is red rust.
facts: Mars looks red because its dust is full of rusty iron minerals.
Hematite's name comes from the Greek word for blood, because the powder is blood-red.
Red ochre, an iron oxide, was among the first paints people ever used, in cave art tens of thousands of years ago.

details.what: Iron ions that each gave up 3 electrons, in a grid with oxide ions. Red-brown rust.
details.where: Rusty cars, red soil and red bricks, and iron ore mines.
details.bonds: Rust's grid takes up more room than the iron it came from, so it cracks and flakes off. That lets air and water reach fresh metal, and rust keeps spreading. Aluminum's oxide skin, by contrast, seals itself.
details.extra: Thermite is iron oxide mixed with aluminum powder. Aluminum steals the oxygen so violently that melted iron pours out.

rankWhy: Rust, and the iron ore that steel is made from.

name: Magnetite
blurb: A mix of Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions with oxygen. Naturally magnetic.
facts: Lodestones are natural magnetite magnets. Hung on a string, they pointed north and became the first compasses.
Some bacteria grow chains of tiny magnetite crystals and use them like a compass needle.

details.what: A black, heavy iron oxide with a mix of iron ions, some that gave 2 electrons and some 3.
details.where: Iron ore mines, black sand on beaches, and the dark finish on 'blued' steel tools and gun parts.
details.bonds: Electrons hop back and forth between the 2+ and 3+ irons. That hopping lets magnetite carry some electricity, unlike most rocks.
details.extra: Cooling lava locks in the direction its magnetite points. Those rocks showed that Earth's magnetic poles have flipped many times.

name: Copper(II) oxide
blurb: Copper gives 2, oxygen takes 2. The black tarnish on hot copper.
facts: Copper oxides give glass and pottery glazes their blue and green colors.
The first 'high-temperature' superconductors, found in 1986, are built around copper-oxide layers.

details.what: A black powder of copper ions that each gave 2 electrons, held with oxide ions.
details.where: The dark tarnish on heated copper pipe, some wood preservatives, and blue-green fireworks.
